content: Perinatal infections in neonates are predominantly bacterial in origin. These infections can be acquired from the mother either before or during birth, or from environmental sources after delivery. Premature infants are particularly susceptible to perinatal infections due to their underdeveloped immune systems. Neonates, especially those born prematurely, have a limited ability to exhibit symptoms, making it crucial to recognize even subtle deviations from normal behavior as potential indicators of bacterial disease. These infections can cause insidious damage to the central nervous system and sensory systems. When symptoms do manifest, they often result in significant mental or sensory impairments, or both. Perinatal infections occurring within the first few days to 14 days of life are typically caused by exposure to pathogens present in the cervico-vaginal canal during delivery. The mortality and morbidity associated with both acute and chronic perinatal infections are notably high, necessitating prompt and aggressive diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. The pathogens responsible for early-onset perinatal infections include: Escherichia coli Group B beta-hemolytic Streptococci Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gonococci) Listeria monocytogenes Bacteroides species Candida albicans Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Herpes Simplex Virus Type-2 (HSV-2) Late-onset perinatal infections, which typically occur 3 to 6 weeks after birth, are caused by environmental pathogens. These include: Klebsiella species Aerobacter species Proteus species Staphylococcus aureus Haemophilus influenzae Pseudomonas aeruginosa Coxsackie B virus Candida albicans Echovirus Influenza virus Parainfluenza virus Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) Several vertically transmitted infections are grouped under the TORCH complex: T: Toxoplasmosis caused by Toxoplasma gondii O: Other infections (detailed below) R: Rubella C: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) H: Herpes Simplex Virus Type-2 (neonatal herpes simplex) The Other infections category includes: Parvovirus B19 Coxsackie virus Chickenpox (caused by Varicella Zoster Virus) Chlamydia infection HIV Human T-lymphotropic virus Syphilis Zika virus infection, which can lead to microcephaly and other brain defects in the child Hepatitis B Diagnosis and treatment of perinatal infections require a systematic and aggressive approach to minimize the risk of severe complications.
